title: 道德經 第七十三章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 73, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 89. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 73 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 任為 (Leaving Action Alone). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

morph.gloss: bold, daring — the nerve to act
in, at (the all-purpose preposition, here setting out the field the boldness works in)
daring — the verb 'to dare' standing as a noun
to kill — and with no passive marker, equally 'to be killed'; see the note

sentences.i: Boldness that dares gets a man killed;
sentences.n:
Chinese has no passive. 則殺 is 'then kill / then killed' and nothing in the grammar chooses; only sense does, and the parallel line's 活 'lives' settles it — the daring man is the one who ends up dead. Wang Bi settles it too, glossing this line 必不得其死也, 'he will surely not get his own death' — the old phrase for dying by violence rather than in your bed.

於 after an adjective marks the field it operates in: bold *in* daring, as against bold *in* not-daring. The two lines differ by one character and end opposite.

The couplet rhymed. 殺 and 活 were both entering-tone words of the 月 group, closing on a -t stop, and 害 in the next unit belongs to the same rhyme group (in its departing-tone half). Mandarin has worn every one of those endings off — shā, huó, hài chime not at all — so this is one of the places where the poem is audible only to the eye.

sentences.i: boldness that does not dare keeps him alive.
sentences.n:
Both lines begin 勇, and that is the point. The book is not against nerve; it is against one of the two things nerve can be spent on. Holding back takes the same courage as going forward and gets no credit for it, which is why the text has to say 勇 twice rather than set courage against cowardice.

敢 is chapter 67's word — 不敢為天下先, 'not daring to be first under heaven' — where not-daring was named one of the three treasures.

morph.gloss: the two of them, this pair
the one that — turns what precedes into a noun
in the one case ——  (not the modern Mandarin 'or')
to benefit, to do good to

sentences.l:
These two:
the one benefits, the other harms.
sentences.n: 或 ... 或 is 'in one case ... in the other', a distributive pair, and it is worth unlearning the modern Mandarin sense here: 或 is not 'or'. Nothing in the line says which of the two is which, and after two lines that seemed to have settled it, that reticence is deliberate — it is the step into the next unit, where even the sage stops claiming to know what heaven is for and against.

sentences.t:
天之所惡，
孰知其故？
是以聖人猶難之。

morph.gloss: heaven — sky and the order that runs it, in one word
that which is —— : makes a noun of the verb after it
to hate, to loathe (read wù; read è the same character is the adjective 'ugly, bad')
who? which one? — the interrogative pronoun, at the head of its clause
the reason, the cause — 故 as a noun, not the usual 'therefore'
therefore, and so — a fused connective; neither half gives you it alone
the sage — in this book the ruler who holds the Way, not a moral saint
to treat as difficult, to refuse to find it easy — the adjective as a verb (nán)
it — the object pronoun, not the genitive 'of'

sentences.l:
What heaven hates —
who knows its reason?
Therefore the sage still treats it as difficult.
sentences.i: What heaven hates — who knows the reason for it? Even the sage does not find this easy.
sentences.n:
所 before a verb makes a noun of it: 所惡 is 'what is hated', as 所居 and 所生 were 'what is dwelt in' and 'what is lived by' one chapter back. And 惡 is the polyphone that changes word with its sense — è, 'ugly', in chapters 2 and 20; wù, 'to hate', here and in chapter 8's 眾人之所惡.

故 is doing its other job. Everywhere else in this book it opens a consequence, 'therefore'; here it is the noun the consequence comes from, a reason. 孰知其故 asks for the reason and does not expect it.

是以聖人猶難之 is word for word chapter 63's line, and what 之 points at is not said. Wang Bi points it at the daring: his comment runs 夫聖人之明，猶難於勇敢，況無聖人之明而欲行之乎 — 'even the sage's clear sight still finds bold daring hard; how much more a man without it who means to go ahead' — so the sage's hesitation is about acting, not about the puzzle of what heaven hates. Read it the other way and 之 is the question itself. The English leaves 'it' open, as the Chinese does. And because the line fits chapter 63 so exactly, it has long been suspected of drifting into this chapter from that one — an honest possibility, not a settled fact, and the received text keeps it.

sentences.t:
天之道，
不爭而善勝，

morph.gloss: to contend, to fight for place
to be good at — the adjective 'good' as a verb, standing before what it is good at

sentences.l:
The way of heaven:
does not contend, and yet is good at overcoming;
sentences.n:
善 + verb, 'good at ——ing', is the frame the next four lines are built on, each of them a 不 X 而善 Y: does not do the obvious thing, and is good at what the obvious thing was for. The subject is stated once, in 天之道, and then dropped for the rest of the passage, as Chinese drops any subject the topic has already supplied.

不爭 is the book's oldest refrain — chapter 8's water, chapter 22's 夫唯不爭，故天下莫能與之爭, chapter 66's rivers and seas. Here it is heaven that wins by it.

morph.gloss: to answer, to respond to a call (yìng; distinguish yīng 'ought to', not the sense here)

sentences.l: does not speak, and yet is good at answering;
sentences.n: 應 is answering as a bell answers the stick or a valley answers a shout — response, not initiative. Heaven says nothing first and always replies, which is chapter 23's 希言自然 seen from the other side.

morph.gloss: to summon, to call in — the word for a lord calling a man to court
of itself, of their own accord — here the adverb, not the reflexive object 'himself'

sentences.l: does not summon, and yet they come of themselves;
sentences.i: it issues no summons, and yet everything comes of its own accord;
sentences.n:
自 was 'himself' in chapter 72's 自知不自見, the reflexive object standing before its verb. Here the same character is the adverb: of itself, of its own accord — the 自 of 自然, 'so of itself'. Position does not distinguish them; only what the verb needs does.

And who comes? The line does not say. Chinese leaves the subject out whenever the topic covers it, and English has to put something back — 'they', 'everything'. What is meant is what always comes when nothing is demanded: the ten thousand things.

召 is a technical word, the summons a ruler issues; the line is measuring heaven against a court that has to send for people.

morph.gloss: slack, loose — of a belt left untightened; a rare character, see the note
——ly, in that manner: attached to a word it makes an adverb of it
to plan, to take counsel about, to deal with a thing by forethought

sentences.l: slack, and yet good at planning.
sentences.i: it takes its ease, and yet it is good at laying its plans.
sentences.n:
繟 is rare enough that its sense here has to be argued rather than looked up. The old dictionaries give 'slack, loose', said of a belt not pulled tight; Wang Bi reads it as unhurried, glossing the line with a heaven that hangs out its signs of fortune and misfortune before the event, so that it never has to hurry. Other editions print 坦然 tǎn rán, 'level, open, unruffled', which lands in much the same place. The received Wang Bi text prints 繟 and this is that text.

X然 is the standing way to make a manner-word: 然 is 'so, thus', and stuck to an adjective it gives '——ly'. You have met it inside 自然 itself, 'so of itself'.

The four lines rhyme in pairs. 勝 and 應 both belonged to the 蒸 group and still chime in Mandarin (shèng, yìng); 來 and 謀 both belonged to the 之 group and no longer chime at all (lái, móu). Half the sound survives, which is about the usual rate.

sentences.t:
天網恢恢，
疏而不失。

morph.gloss: vast and vast — a doubled word: wide, and wide again, wide all the way out
wide-meshed, loosely woven — the physical sense behind the 疏 that elsewhere means 'to hold at a distance'

sentences.l:
Heaven's net is vast and vast;
wide-meshed, and yet it loses nothing.
sentences.i: Heaven's net is wide, and wide again; the weave is loose, and nothing gets away from it.
sentences.n:
Doubling an adjective is the classical way of spreading it over the whole of what it describes — not 'very wide' but wide and wide again, wide all the way out. English has no tidy equivalent and the literal keeps the doubling.

疏 is the same character that means 'to hold at arm's length, to treat as a stranger' in chapter 56's 不可得而疏. Here it is the weaver's sense that the other one grew out of: a loose weave, big gaps. The gaps are the argument — heaven catches everything without gripping anything, which is what the whole chapter has been saying about not contending, not speaking, not summoning.

The couplet outlived the book. It is still a current proverb in Chinese, usually quoted with 漏 'to leak' in place of 失: the net is wide, and yet nothing gets out through the gaps.
